newsitem.title: UK: Dlr cruises under multi-year peaks in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dlr cruises under multi-year peaks in late Europe.

text.p: The dollar traded calmly in late Europe below earlier multiple-year highs, thirsty for more gains but blocked by a raft of bids above 1.84 marks, traders said.
Dollar/mark shot to a new six-year peak of 1.8403 marks in morning Europe, drawing fresh momentum as a fiery dollar/Swiss powered to its highest level in almost four years.
"People are still looking for dollars and the cheapest dollar to buy is against the Swiss franc," said a spot trader at a U.S. bank in London.
The dollar stood at 1.8369/74 marks and 1.5138/48 Swiss francs at 1458 GMT versus 1.8310/20 and 1.5018/23 late Thursday.
Dollar/Swiss earlier hit 1.5176, its highest level since August 1993.
Dollar/yen shook off some of its recent lethargy, pushing to a six-week peak of 116.83 in late trade, up from its previous close here of 115.87/92.
Traders said a mark/yen rally had helped boost dollar/yen.

The mark stayed generally soft on the crosses, though, as the market remained convinced that European monetary union will begin on time in 1999 and usher in a broad-based, soft euro. That sentiment -- and thus the mark's weakness -- shows no signs of disappearing, traders and analysts said.

"Unless Europe blows up, people are going to keep selling marks," said one trader. "And even if we see a meltdown in EMU and it doesn't go ahead, mark buying will be short-lived because the Germans need low interest rates to boost growth."

The Bundesbank's move yesterday to set a repo for just two weeks of its four-week summer recess gave the market brief pause for thought, however, suggesting that the bank was prepared to adjust monetary policy if need be.
Bundesbank member Reimut Jochimsen was quoted today as saying the bank was "driving carefully" in the current environment.

"Like many German holidaymakers who are staying at home this summer on account of the weak mark, so too will the Bundesbank. This should keep the markets guessing as to the likely timing of a switch to a variable rate repo," said Michael Lewis, senior international economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell here.
Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum told a newspaper today that the dollar was slightly overvalued, but no major inflationary pressures were apparent at present.
U.S. data out today supported the dollar. June durable goods orders rose 2.3 percent, well above the 1.4 percent the market had been expecting.
The drop in orders in May was revised to 0.4 from 0.7 percent.

Existing home sales declined by 2.6 percent to an annualized rate of 4.14 million -- versus a consensus forecast of 4.19 million -- but analysts said high consumer confidence and declining mortgage rates should bolster sales farther out.

After this week's frugal data diet, next week promises a feast of key U.S. figures for the market. The employment cost index on Tuesday, GDP on Thursday and the closely-watched non-farm payrolls due Friday, are expected to confirm the picture of robust growth with no obvious inflation.

Elsewhere, mark/Swiss climbed to 82.45/47 centimes by 1539 GMT from late Thursday's European level of 82.00/02. The cross has been exceptionally volatile in the last two days after dollar/Swiss' belated participation in the general dollar rally triggered a short squeeze in mark/Swiss.
Few expect the party to last, however, as EMU concerns come back to haunt the mark and attract safe haven-seeking money into the Swiss franc.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
